I've heard that Ubuntu is shady. I'm a native windows user but want to become familiar, comfortable, and productive with Linux - however, I don't have a clue where to start or what I want to start with.

Edit: Thank you all so much for the advice! I'm going to pore over my options for a couple of days and then post an update...somewhere... once I try it out!
ELI5: How do I and why should I get started with Linux?

I would suggest starting with Ubuntu or Mint (or another Ubuntu-based distribution) because it has more things pre-configured, and so there is less of a barrier to entry. However, Ubuntu has (had?) a relationship with Amazon that basically feeds anything that you type into search to Amazon so they can insert Amazon ads into your results. I don't believe that Mint does this.

As others have said, the best way to try it is to either burn a live DVD/USB or install it in a virtual machine. Once you get a bit more familiar and make a more permanent choice about which distribution you want to go with, then you can install it as your main operating system.

Why should you use it? It's liberating! It presents you with a great opportunity to learn how your computer works and why it works that way. It is also a great way to become familiar with some truly awesome open source alternatives to the programs that you already use, and most of them are completely free. It can give new life to older hardware that struggles to keep up with Windows. There are endless reasons to at least give it a try.

Download an image file of Linux Mint, and use ImgBurn to write the file to a blank DVD. Some versions of Windows can write these files natively, but this bypasses determining if you can. After writing the image to the disk, leave it in the drive, and reboot. Either set your optical drive as you default boot device, or use the appropriate "F key" to select your boot device. If all goes well, the disk should boot, and your live session should load. Here is the manual for the current version of Mint.

As for why.... because, it's free as in freedom, free as in lunch, lots of fun to use, will amaze & astound your friends, and is just generally bad ass. There are great communities of people willing, and able to assist you.

As others have suggested, you can use a live CD. However, if you have a old machine (low spec) laptop or desktop around I would use this to try a few flavours of Linux on that. Try to do something useful with it. Set up a Samba fileserver or Transmission download machine. Ubuntu / Mint, Fedora, Open Suse and try a few.

You could also look at something like this free EdX course on Linux: https://www.edx.org/course/introduction-linux-linuxfoundationx-lfs101x-2

You could also run up a number of virtual machines with different distros on.

It doesn't seem to be mentioned yet, but there is an Ubuntu-based distribution called ElementaryOS. They ask you to pay something when you download but you can enter 0 as an amount to get it for free. Some people don't like the move because one of the heads on the project came off a little harsh when asked about it. Personally, I didn't mind kicking them $10 after I used it for a few months.

Linux is good to learn due to the amount of device OS's that are built off of it. Have a device that won't do this one little thing that it is entirely capable of doing? Have access to the command line? Change it yourself.

I won't speak on distros. I believe everyone else has that covered.

First off, don't worry about distros. At your current skill level, you're probably not going to appreciate the differences in the various distros. What you need to start with is an extremely popular distro whose userbase has posted all the questions you're going to ask, and received answers for most of them. So, throw a dart at ONE of the more popular flavors and don't look back until you think you have a firm understanding of how it all works.

My Windows background started with 3.1 and continued through XP. I abandoned Windows almost entirely around the time that Vista came out; my only experience with the three post-XP versions of windows has been troubleshooting other people's problems. I find Ubuntu's default "Unity" desktop environment to be completely unintuitive. Linux Mint is based heavily on Ubuntu (which is based on Debian), but uses the "Cinnamon" desktop environment by default. I found Cinnamon much more intuitive than Unity, so I would strongly recommend Linux Mint as your first distro. Download it here. If you need help installing it, ask.

Personally, I disagree with the advice to boot from Live CDs/DVDs/USB drives. In my experience, Live CDs are SLOW, which makes the entire experience far less pleasant than it should be. My advice would be to yank your old hard drive out of your computer entirely, stick it in a drawer or put it up on a shelf somewhere for safekeeping, and pop in a nice, shiny, fast, 64GB solid-state drive for your Linux install. The speed increase of an SSD over even a hard drive, let alone an optical drive, will make the experience much more pleasant. You'll be far more likely to want to use Linux when it's considerably faster than your Windows install.

Google is your best friend. Always throw "ubuntu" into your troubleshooting queries, not "linux". If you use "Linux", you'll frequently find commands for Fedora or another distro that simply won't work for Ubuntu/Mint.

Don't be afraid of the shell (command line, terminal window). GUIs are much more capable now than they were when I got started, but for most simple tasks, the shell is much faster and easier to use.

Feel free to PM me if you have any specific questions. I'd be glad to help you get started.

Why? There are many reasons, but they usually end up boiled down to a few. Here are the ones I found compelling:

  1. Philosophy. If you believe that Software ought to be free (either financially, or so you can view/change/redistribute code) then Linux is amazing.

  2. Cost - there is paid Linux software, but it is the exception to the rule. Most of it is completely free.

  3. Security - Linux is not bulletproof, but the amount of end-user targeted malware is almost nil due to its much smaller (and for the most part, technologically competent) user base. Malware is extremely rare, most exploits come from third party bullshit like flash.

  4. Stability - I have seen individual pieces of software crash, poorly written GUIs crash, shitty nvidia drivers that don't support fucking optimus crashing my gui...but I've never had an actual system crash, or been forced to reboot to solve one of those problems. Most I've ever had to do is kill X (restart the GUI).

  5. If you want to be a System Administrator or senior IT guy of some flavour, serious Linux knowledge will boost your paygrade substantially - usually quite a bit better paid than Windows admins.

  6. to be a ninja

As for the how, others in this thread have addressed this in more detail, basically download a live DVD/USB or spin up a VM if you don't have hardware to dedicate to the task. One warning though - if installing it on a system with multiple HDD partitions, be advised that Linux uses a very different and frankly confusing naming scheme for disks - the explanation of why is really more of an advanced topic, just make sure you know what is on what partition before you overwrite anything.

RE: Distros...a lot of people say Ubuntu, I couldn't disagree more emphatically. Ubuntu loves to do shit it's own way - not saying it is a bad OS, but it will teach you shit that is wrong in the rest of the Linux world (how it handles root acct/sudo for instance is very different from any other distro I've tried) and uses components nobody else is (their own brand new display manager, shitfuckingtastic Unity interface, etc). Learn Debian or RHEL or a derivative thereof, or ideally one of both - this will give you working knowledge of like 90% of linux distros. Debian derivatives include Ubuntu, Mint, ElementaryOS...etc. RHEL derivatives include CentOS and Fedora.

They function similarly in many ways, subtle differences in some others. Most obvious difference is package managers (Aptitude aka APT for Debian derivatives, including ubuntu, vs Yum for RHEL derivatives). My personal setup is Debian 8 with the Cinnamon GUI (originates from Mint, my favourite linux GUI by far). I use it as a KVM based Hypervisor, for general office stuff, and as a development environment.

Other useful knowledge:

-Netflix works natively with Chrome in Linux, easiest way to get silverlight working.

-After installing Debian, if you can't install anything from the CLI, check your /etc/apt/sources.list file and make sure the web repositories aren't commented out (if you install from DVD or USB using the graphical installer, it seems to do this...never seen any other distro do it)

-Best office suite is probably LibreOffice, but to be truthful, when I need Excel, I still fire up Office 2013 in a VM.

-GIMP is a great photoshop alternative

-Pidgin is an excellent IM client that supports most popular services.

-Imo, best email client is Thunderbird.

-Blu Ray playback does work but takes a little effort to get up and running, even when using VLC (which basically solves all codec problems for you Windows side <3)
